narrative:
The model predicted a 59% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score of 22.5 was the strongest influence; it sits far below the average of 37.2 among students who were accepted, pushing the prediction heavily toward failure. Your first-year and third-year class rankings came next. Placing in the bottom decile for both Year 1 and Year 3—compared to an average around the middle of the class among accepted students—further increased the estimated risk of failing the bar.

Your high family income worked in the opposite direction, modestly lowering the predicted chance of failure. However, it was not strong enough to overcome the academic signals.

Taken together, the model concluded that the combination of a low LSAT and consistently bottom-decile performance in law school made success on the bar exam unlikely. 

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model flagged. Retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score, while also working to raise your class rank. These improvements would directly address the factors that led to the rejection and improve your chances in a future application. (218 words)
